newsitem.title: USA: U.S. foresees continuity in U.S.-British relations.
newsitem.headline: U.S. foresees continuity in U.S.-British relations.

text.p: The White House predicted on Friday that U.S. President Bill Clinton would have a close, cooperative relationship with Britain's new prime minister, Tony Blair, and rejected suggestions Blair ran a Clinton-style election campaign.
"I foresee continuity in U.S.-U.K. relations," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the day after Blair's Labour Party scored a stunning landslide victory over John Major's Conservatives.
"The president looks forward to working with Prime Minister Blair. But our agenda is one of common purpose and has been and will continue to be," McCurry said.
Clinton called Blair late Thursday night to congratulate him and tried to reach Major. But Major was unavailable at the late hour.
McCurry said Clinton would try to reach Major on Friday "to express the president's appreciation for the very close working relationship he's had with the prime minister."
He cited work that Britain and the United States did on ending the Bosnian conflict, on supporting the Northern Ireland peace process and on charting the future of NATO as important achievements.

Some of Clinton's former political advisers, including his former pollster Stan Greenberg, served discreetly as campaign advisers to Blair and there was criticism in Britain that Blair ran a Clinton-style campaign.
"Oh, I think that was less-than-sophisticated punditry, and not really sophisticated analysis. It's not exactly correct," he said.

Clinton has never forgotten that Major supported then-President George Bush over him in the 1992 election. Conservative Party members rummaged through passport files to see if they could find any embarrassing information on Clinton that would help Bush.
McCurry said Clinton had long since put that behind him.
"He worked very closely with Prime Minister Major, has a great deal of affection for him and we expect that will continue," he said.

The spokesman said he did not know whether Clinton and Blair would meet before leaders of the United States, Britain, Canada, Italy, Germany, France and Japan meet in Denver June 20-22 for the annual economic summit of the Group of Seven.
